script.opening: (Calm but tense, slightly guarded; glances around the room now and then.) "I stopped my antipsychotic a few months back — I felt fine and I hated the side-effects. But this last couple of weeks I can feel it creeping back — the thoughts, not sleeping, getting suspicious. I recognise it now. I want to go back on the medication before it gets bad. Can you just prescribe it for me today?"

facts.text: "Same as before, the start of it. Feeling people are watching me, talking about me. I know it's the illness, but it's getting louder." Neighbours "might be" talking about him. About two weeks.
"Not voices. Not yet." If asked about harming himself or others: "No. Nothing like that. That's why I want to catch it now." No plans, no weapons, no command thoughts.
"Sleep's bad — a few hours. I'm getting by." Still going to work, eating, washing.
"Nothing new, no" — no cannabis for 3 years, a few beers at weekends.

Was on olanzapine 10 mg at night for 4 years; stopped it himself 5 months ago. "I felt like a zombie, and the weight" — gained 12 kg on it. Didn't tell his team; was discharged to GP care 18 months ago. Has the community mental health team number somewhere.
No heart problems, no fainting, no diabetes known. No regular medicines. No allergies. Smokes 15 a day.
Delivery van driver. If asked: "Why do you ask?" — then accepts advice not to drive while unwell.
First episode at 26, two admissions (last one 6 years ago, under section). Lives alone; sister nearby is supportive.
"Ending up back in hospital. Losing control. Last time was awful."

Calm, insightful, wants speed: "As long as it's quick." If the doctor refuses without a plan: "So you won't prescribe it?" — becomes frustrated and may say he'll "manage on his own". If the doctor explains a same-day call to his team: "How long will that take?" then "Fine, if it gets me on it." Interested to hear there are other medicines: "I didn't know there was a choice."

ice.ideas: "I'm relapsing — the same tablet again will stop it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of another hospital admission and losing control; the weight gain and feeling "like a zombie" that made him stop.
ice.expectations: "Just the prescription, so I can get on with it."

cues: "I recognise it now." — insight to praise.
"I hated the side-effects." — invites a choice of medicine.
"Last time was awful." — the fear driving the urgency.

checkpoints.text: VALIDATES the insight — recognising early relapse and seeking treatment is a positive step to support — rather than meeting it with a bureaucratic refusal

Assesses CURRENT mental state and RELAPSE/RISK (symptoms, insight, function, risk to self/others, command symptoms) and escalates URGENTLY to crisis team/CMHT/psychiatry if acutely unwell or at significant risk

Understands WHO PRESCRIBES — the NICE CG178 relapse route back to secondary care, and (NHS England 2018) the clinician who starts or changes a medicine is responsible for it; restarting after a long gap with relapse needs PSYCHIATRIC involvement (re-referral/liaison) to choose drug and dose, after which the GP can prescribe — not a unilateral GP reissue

Arranges the NICE CG178 BASELINE MONITORING face to face — weight/BMI/waist, BP/pulse, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement-disorder assessment, diet and activity — with an ECG only if the SPC requires it, there is cardiovascular risk or history, or he is admitted — as part of safe restarting
Explores WHY he stopped (side-effects, adherence) and discusses side-effect management, relapse risk, and options (e.g. depot/alternative agent) toward sustainable treatment
Honours his insight and urgency, and explains that involving his mental-health team is to get him safe treatment FAST — not a brush-off — keeping him engaged
Balances a supportive response with the proper process, neither bluntly refusing (risking disengagement/relapse) nor unsafely reissuing
Safety-nets and follows up: urgent escalation if at risk, psychiatric re-referral/liaison, baseline monitoring arranged, crisis contacts/red flags, and review — swift, safe, shared-care restarting

worked.txt: "First — well done for recognising this and coming in early. Spotting your own warning signs and wanting to act before things worsen is exactly the right thing, and it’s genuinely impressive. Let’s get you the right help quickly."

"Tell me more about what’s coming back — the thoughts, the suspiciousness, the sleep. Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else? How are you managing day to day? … I need to understand how things are right now."

"I want to act fast, but I also want to do it safely. After a few months off, with things creeping back, the guidance is for your mental-health team to see you and choose the right drug and dose for you — then I can prescribe it once that’s agreed. That’s not a brush-off; it’s how we get you treated properly and quickly."

"Because you’re noticing it creeping back, I’m going to contact your mental-health team / the crisis team today to get you seen urgently, so we don’t lose time. If things were more advanced or risky, that would be even more urgent."

"Let’s also get the baseline checks these medicines need — I’ll book you in at the surgery for your weight, waist and blood pressure and some bloods for sugar, cholesterol and prolactin, and we’ll check for any stiffness or restlessness; a heart tracing only if your team or the medicine needs one. And tell me which side-effects you hated — because we can often choose or adjust to avoid them, so you’re not back here in six months having stopped again."

"While we get you seen: here are the crisis numbers. If the thoughts get worse, you can’t sleep at all, you feel unsafe, or anyone’s worried about you, contact them or go to A&E. I’ll chase the referral and we’ll stay on top of this together."

f.learning: A patient who recognises early relapse of psychosis and proactively asks to restart their antipsychotic is showing valuable insight that should be strongly supported — the task is to act on his relapse signs both quickly AND safely, holding a supportive response together with the proper process, never meeting it with a bureaucratic refusal. Assess his current mental state and relapse (returning symptoms, insight, function) and crucially the risk to himself (self-harm, self-neglect) and others, plus any command symptoms; if he is acutely unwell or at significant risk this is urgent, warranting contact with the crisis team/CMHT or urgent psychiatric assessment rather than a prescription. Understand who prescribes: NICE CG178 directs a person with established psychosis showing signs of relapse back to secondary care (crisis team or CMHT), and NHS England guidance (2018) makes the clinician who starts or changes a medicine responsible for it — formal shared-care agreements cover only some antipsychotics, such as clozapine — so restarting after a months-long gap with relapse generally needs psychiatric involvement — re-referral to the CMHT or liaison with his mental-health team — rather than a unilateral GP reissue of a higher-risk drug, framed as getting him the right, safe treatment fast rather than a brush-off. Arrange the NICE CG178 baseline monitoring face to face — weight/BMI and waist, blood pressure and pulse, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, an assessment of movement disorders, and diet and physical activity, with an ECG only if the product information requires it, there is cardiovascular risk on examination or a personal cardiovascular history, or he is being admitted — and remember clozapine is specialist-only with additional strict neutrophil monitoring. Explore why he stopped (side-effects such as weight gain, sedation, sexual/metabolic effects or akathisia, and his adherence pattern), discuss managing side-effects and the relapse risk of stopping, and consider options like a long-acting depot or a different agent toward sustainable treatment. The hidden agenda is genuine fear of becoming unwell again, alongside fear of hospital, lost control, judgement and the side-effects that drove him off; honour his insight, act swiftly, explain that involving his mental-health team is to help, and neither bluntly refuse (risking disengagement and relapse) nor unsafely reissue, but escalate appropriately and supportively.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG178 (psychosis and schizophrenia in adults, 2014) · [2] NHS England, Responsibility for prescribing between primary and secondary/tertiary care (2018) · [3] DVLA, Assessing fitness to drive: psychiatric disorders
knowledge.summary: A man with established psychosis who recognises early relapse and asks to restart treatment is doing the right thing. Assess mental state and risk today, get his mental-health team to review him urgently, and set up the physical baseline so a restart is safe.

points.t: NICE CG178 [1]: a person with an established diagnosis who shows signs of relapse should be referred back to secondary care (crisis team or community mental health team). The urgency depends on risk and how far the relapse has progressed.

Current symptoms (sleep, suspiciousness, the “thoughts”), insight, function, substance use, and risk to self and others including command hallucinations. Acute risk means same-day crisis-team contact, not a routine referral.

NHS England 2018 [2]: the clinician who starts or changes a medicine takes responsibility for it until any agreed transfer. After months off treatment with relapse, the choice of drug and dose sits with the specialist; the GP can prescribe once that is agreed.

CG178 [1]: before an antipsychotic, record weight (BMI), waist, pulse and blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders, and diet and activity. ECG if the product information requires it, examination finds cardiovascular risk, there is personal cardiovascular history, or the person is being admitted.

CG178 [1]: weight weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly; pulse, BP, glucose, HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly. Primary care holds the annual physical-health review.

CG178 [1] names no preferred antipsychotic: choose with the person, driven by side effects (metabolic, sedation, sexual, extrapyramidal, akathisia) and previous response. A long-acting injection is an option where the person prefers it. Clozapine is specialist-only with mandatory blood monitoring (BNF).
DVLA [3]: psychotic illness has notification rules for Group 1 and Group 2 licences, and he should not drive if symptoms affect his driving. Check the current DVLA guidance.

Sleep, self-care, work and daily function, support, substance use, and driving.
CG178 baseline: weight, waist, pulse, BP, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated.
Early relapse of established psychosis versus substance-related symptoms or an organic cause.
Direct questions on self-harm, harm to others and command hallucinations; crisis route if risk rises.
Named early relapse with good insight and low immediate risk on current history.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Urgent CMHT review requested today; GP to prescribe once the specialist choice is agreed; baseline checks booked.
Side-effect history passed to the team; long-acting option raised; substance use asked without judgement.
Crisis contacts given; no driving until reviewed; follow-up call in two days.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I hated the side effects” and “before it gets bad” and explored both.
Idea (a GP prescription today), concern (hospital, losing control, side effects), expectation (quick restart).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of another hospital admission and losing control; the weight gain and feeling "like a zombie" that made him stop — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Dominic, I’m Dr Okafor. Thanks for getting in touch. Tell me what’s been happening.

I stopped my antipsychotic a few months back — felt fine and hated the side effects. The last couple of weeks it’s creeping back. The thoughts, not sleeping, getting suspicious. I want to go back on it before it gets bad. Can you just prescribe it today?

First, well done for spotting this so early and reaching out — that’s exactly the right thing to do. I want to help you get back on treatment quickly and safely. Can I ask some questions about how things are right now, and then we’ll agree the fastest safe route?
model.why: Validates insight and sets the agenda honestly

model.text: Yeah, okay. As long as it’s quick.
Tell me about the thoughts that are coming back — what are they like?
Same as before, the start of it. Feeling people are watching me, talking about me. I know it’s the illness, but it’s getting louder.
Are you hearing any voices, and if so, are they telling you to do anything?
Not voices. Not yet.
I ask everyone this: have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else because of what you’re feeling?
model.why: Direct risk assessment to self and others

model.text: No. Nothing like that. That’s why I want to catch it now.
How’s your sleep, and are you managing day to day — eating, looking after yourself?
Sleep’s bad — a few hours. I’m getting by.
Any alcohol or drugs, including cannabis, recently?
Nothing new, no.
Thanks. If that ever changes, tell me or your team without worrying about being judged — it can affect how the medicine works.
You said you hated the side effects. Which ones bothered you most?
I felt like a zombie, and the weight. That’s why I stopped.
That’s really important, because it shapes what we choose this time. What worries you most about things right now?
Ending up back in hospital. Losing control. Last time was awful.
That makes complete sense, and it’s exactly why acting early is so valuable. What were you hoping would happen today?
model.why: Links the fear to the plan and elicits expectations

model.text: Just the prescription, so I can get on with it.

Here’s my honest thinking. You’ve been off it for months, the warning signs are back, and the side effects were bad enough to stop you. Choosing the right medicine and dose now is a specialist decision, and your mental-health team can see you quickly.
model.why: Explains why restart needs specialist input

model.text: So you won’t prescribe it?

I’m not saying no. I’m saying I want it right. I’ll contact your team today and ask for an urgent review. If they advise restarting your previous medicine or a different one, I can prescribe it as soon as it’s agreed, so you’re not waiting.
model.why: Keeps him engaged: not a refusal, a faster safe route

model.text: How long will that take?
I’ll ask for days, not weeks, and I’ll tell them you’re asking for help early. If things get worse before then, the crisis team can see you the same day.

While we wait, I’d like some baseline checks that these medicines need: weight, waist, blood pressure and pulse, and blood tests for sugar, cholesterol and a hormone called prolactin. We may also do a heart tracing, depending on the medicine and your heart risk.
Fine, if it gets me on it.
And I’ll tell your team about the zombie feeling and the weight, so they can pick something with fewer of those effects — or talk to you about an injection if you’d prefer that to daily tablets.
model.why: Shares side-effect history to guide a sustainable choice

model.text: I didn’t know there was a choice.
There is, and your view counts. One more thing: are you driving at the moment?
model.why: Raises DVLA fitness to drive neutrally

model.text: Why do you ask?
Because with your sleep this poor and the thoughts coming back, if you do drive, please don’t until your team has reviewed you. We can go through the DVLA rules together once you’re settled.

If the thoughts get stronger, voices start, you stop sleeping altogether, or you ever feel unsafe or someone is worried about you, contact the crisis line or 111 and choose the mental-health option straight away, or go to A&E. I’ll text you the numbers.
Okay.
Can you tell me the plan in your own words?
You’re ringing my team today for a quick review, I’ll do the bloods and checks, no driving, and crisis line if it gets worse.
Spot on. I’ll call you in two days to check the team has been in touch.

social.t: People who stop antipsychotics often do so because of side effects. A non-judgemental response keeps him engaged at the point he is asking for help.
Cannabis and other substances are common relapse precipitants. Ask, respect a refusal, and leave the door open.

legal.t: Psychotic illness has DVLA notification rules for Group 1 and Group 2 licences; advise him not to drive while symptoms affect his driving, and check current DVLA guidance.
He has insight and capacity. Share information with his mental-health team for his care; involve others only with consent unless risk rises.

professional.t: NHS England (2018): the clinician who starts or changes a medicine is responsible until an agreed transfer. GMC Good practice in prescribing: prescribe only when you have adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and the medicine is serving his needs.
NICE CG178: primary care holds the annual physical-health check for people with psychosis; record baseline and follow-up monitoring.

community.t: Local crisis team, NHS 111 mental-health option, and peer support through Rethink Mental Illness or Mind.

redFlags: Thoughts of harming self or others
Severe self-neglect or not sleeping at all
ice: Idea: “The GP can just restart it today.”
Concern: hospital, losing control, and the side effects

playbook.diagnosis: “This sounds like the early signs of your illness returning. You’ve spotted it early and you’re safe right now, which gives us time to do this properly and quickly.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as the smoke alarm going off before there’s a fire. You heard it. Now we want the right people to choose the right extinguisher quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about ending up in hospital, and you stopped because you felt like a zombie. Both of those are why I want your team to help choose the medicine this time.”
management.psychosocial: Frame the referral as speed, not refusal; share his side-effect history; raise a long-acting option; advise on driving and substance use without judgement.
sharedPlan: Contact the CMHT today for urgent review; crisis team if risk rises
GP to prescribe once the specialist choice is agreed
CG178 baseline: weight, waist, pulse, BP, glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated
safetyNet: Crisis line, NHS 111 mental-health option or A&E if worse or unsafe
Follow-up call in two days; no driving until reviewed

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed at either extreme: a bureaucratic refusal that loses the patient, or a repeat prescription without assessment. The marks are for holding speed and safety together.

items.fail: Opening with “I can’t prescribe that” before hearing him out.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He has done the right thing and is met with a barrier.
items.fix: Praise the early help-seeking first, then explain the route.

items.fail: No direct risk questions because he seems calm and insightful.
items.why: Insight does not remove risk. “Fails to assess risk” is a standard Tasks failure in mental-health stations.
items.fix: Ask plainly about harm to self, harm to others and command hallucinations.

items.fail: Reissuing the old antipsychotic on repeat today with no baseline checks.
items.why: NICE CG178 requires baseline physical monitoring, and after months off with relapse the choice is a specialist one.
items.fix: Contact the team today, offer to prescribe once agreed, and book the CG178 baseline.

items.fail: Ordering an ECG, FBC, U&E and LFTs as a reflex and missing prolactin, waist and movement disorders.
items.why: The CG178 baseline list is specific; the ECG depends on the drug and cardiovascular risk.
items.fix: Weight, waist, pulse, BP, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated.

items.why: The reason he stopped is the reason he will stop again. Not exploring it loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “Which side effects bothered you most?” — then pass it to the team and mention alternatives.

items.fail: Ending with “the team will be in touch” and no crisis plan.
items.why: A relapsing patient without crisis contacts or follow-up is an unsafe close.
items.fix: Crisis numbers, teach-back, and a follow-up call in two days.

timeMap.d: He opens with a request. Praise the early help-seeking before anything else, then agree the agenda.
Current symptoms, voices and commands, harm to self or others, sleep, self-care, substances.
Why he stopped (sedation, weight), fear of hospital and losing control, wish for a quick restart.
Specialist choice after months off; GP contacts the team today and prescribes once agreed. Baseline checks. Side-effect history passed on. Driving.
Crisis contacts, teach-back, follow-up call in two days.

wordPics.fail: Either prints the old prescription without any assessment or monitoring, or says flatly “you need to see psychiatry” and ends the call; no risk questions; ignores the side effects that made him stop.
wordPics.pass: Praises his insight, asks about risk and symptoms, explains why the mental-health team should guide the restart, requests an urgent review, and arranges baseline checks with a crisis safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: frames the referral as the faster safe route and offers to prescribe once agreed; uses his side-effect history to shape a better choice; raises a long-acting option; handles substance use and driving without judgement; teach-back and a dated follow-up.

avoid.dont: “I can’t prescribe that — you’ll have to go back to psychiatry.”
avoid.instead: “I want to get you back on treatment quickly and safely. I’ll contact your team today, and I can prescribe as soon as we’ve agreed the right medicine.”
avoid.why: A flat refusal risks losing a man who is asking for help early.

avoid.dont: “No problem, I’ll put the same tablets back on repeat.”
avoid.instead: “Before we restart, let’s check how you are right now and get the checks these medicines need.”
avoid.why: An unmonitored restart without risk assessment or specialist input is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “You shouldn’t have stopped it in the first place.”
avoid.instead: “The side effects were clearly hard. Let’s make sure this time the medicine suits you.”
avoid.why: Blame damages trust and makes the next stop more likely.

points.t: NICE CG178 [1]: a person with an established diagnosis who shows signs of relapse should be referred back to secondary care (crisis team or community mental health team). The urgency depends on risk and how far the relapse has progressed.

Current symptoms (sleep, suspiciousness, the “thoughts”), insight, function, substance use, and risk to self and others including command hallucinations. Acute risk means same-day crisis-team contact, not a routine referral.

NHS England 2018 [2]: the clinician who starts or changes a medicine takes responsibility for it until any agreed transfer. After months off treatment with relapse, the choice of drug and dose sits with the specialist; the GP can prescribe once that is agreed.

CG178 [1]: before an antipsychotic, record weight (BMI), waist, pulse and blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders, and diet and activity. ECG if the product information requires it, examination finds cardiovascular risk, there is personal cardiovascular history, or the person is being admitted.

CG178 [1]: weight weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly; pulse, BP, glucose, HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly. Primary care holds the annual physical-health review.

CG178 [1] names no preferred antipsychotic: choose with the person, driven by side effects (metabolic, sedation, sexual, extrapyramidal, akathisia) and previous response. A long-acting injection is an option where the person prefers it. Clozapine is specialist-only with mandatory blood monitoring (BNF).
DVLA [3]: psychotic illness has notification rules for Group 1 and Group 2 licences, and he should not drive if symptoms affect his driving. Check the current DVLA guidance.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; affirmed his early help-seeking before discussing the request.
Sleep, self-care, work and daily function, support, substance use, and driving.
Picked up “I hated the side effects” and “before it gets bad” and explored both.
Idea (a GP prescription today), concern (hospital, losing control, side effects), expectation (quick restart).
CG178 baseline: weight, waist, pulse, BP, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated.
Early relapse of established psychosis versus substance-related symptoms or an organic cause.
Direct questions on self-harm, harm to others and command hallucinations; crisis route if risk rises.
Named early relapse with good insight and low immediate risk on current history.
Urgent CMHT review requested today; GP to prescribe once the specialist choice is agreed; baseline checks booked.
Side-effect history passed to the team; long-acting option raised; substance use asked without judgement.
Crisis contacts given; no driving until reviewed; follow-up call in two days.

social.t: People who stop antipsychotics often do so because of side effects. A non-judgemental response keeps him engaged at the point he is asking for help.
Cannabis and other substances are common relapse precipitants. Ask, respect a refusal, and leave the door open.

legal.t: Psychotic illness has DVLA notification rules for Group 1 and Group 2 licences; advise him not to drive while symptoms affect his driving, and check current DVLA guidance.
He has insight and capacity. Share information with his mental-health team for his care; involve others only with consent unless risk rises.

professional.t: NHS England (2018): the clinician who starts or changes a medicine is responsible until an agreed transfer. GMC Good practice in prescribing: prescribe only when you have adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and the medicine is serving his needs.
NICE CG178: primary care holds the annual physical-health check for people with psychosis; record baseline and follow-up monitoring.

community.t: Local crisis team, NHS 111 mental-health option, and peer support through Rethink Mental Illness or Mind.

redFlags: Thoughts of harming self or others
Severe self-neglect or not sleeping at all
ice: Idea: “The GP can just restart it today.”
Concern: hospital, losing control, and the side effects

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like the early signs of your illness returning. You’ve spotted it early and you’re safe right now, which gives us time to do this properly and quickly.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as the smoke alarm going off before there’s a fire. You heard it. Now we want the right people to choose the right extinguisher quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about ending up in hospital, and you stopped because you felt like a zombie. Both of those are why I want your team to help choose the medicine this time.”
management.psychosocial: Frame the referral as speed, not refusal; share his side-effect history; raise a long-acting option; advise on driving and substance use without judgement.
sharedPlan: Contact the CMHT today for urgent review; crisis team if risk rises
GP to prescribe once the specialist choice is agreed
CG178 baseline: weight, waist, pulse, BP, glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated
safetyNet: Crisis line, NHS 111 mental-health option or A&E if worse or unsafe
Follow-up call in two days; no driving until reviewed

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed at either extreme: a bureaucratic refusal that loses the patient, or a repeat prescription without assessment. The marks are for holding speed and safety together.

items.fail: Opening with “I can’t prescribe that” before hearing him out.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He has done the right thing and is met with a barrier.
items.fix: Praise the early help-seeking first, then explain the route.

items.fail: No direct risk questions because he seems calm and insightful.
items.why: Insight does not remove risk. “Fails to assess risk” is a standard Tasks failure in mental-health stations.
items.fix: Ask plainly about harm to self, harm to others and command hallucinations.

items.fail: Reissuing the old antipsychotic on repeat today with no baseline checks.
items.why: NICE CG178 requires baseline physical monitoring, and after months off with relapse the choice is a specialist one.
items.fix: Contact the team today, offer to prescribe once agreed, and book the CG178 baseline.

items.fail: Ordering an ECG, FBC, U&E and LFTs as a reflex and missing prolactin, waist and movement disorders.
items.why: The CG178 baseline list is specific; the ECG depends on the drug and cardiovascular risk.
items.fix: Weight, waist, pulse, BP, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders; ECG where indicated.

items.why: The reason he stopped is the reason he will stop again. Not exploring it loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “Which side effects bothered you most?” — then pass it to the team and mention alternatives.

items.fail: Ending with “the team will be in touch” and no crisis plan.
items.why: A relapsing patient without crisis contacts or follow-up is an unsafe close.
items.fix: Crisis numbers, teach-back, and a follow-up call in two days.
